exam_format.format: Mostly written answers, ONE multiple choice question, no negative marking

source_priority: Past paper examples worked through in revision lecture (HIGHEST FIDELITY to actual exam)
Further Sample Questions (closer to exam difficulty)
Study Notes Practice Questions (curated revision questions)

questions.source_label: Past Paper Example (worked in revision lecture)
questions.question_text: Explain why it is difficult to track the performance of a direct organic CGM, and suggest one method by which a startup could detect where an organic CGM existed for its product and was operating effectively.
questions.model_answer: It is difficult to track because organic CGMs are word-of-mouth referrals — there is no invitation link or button to click on, so you cannot trace the referral back to its source (1 mark). One detection method: monitor for non-linear (exponential) rises in homepage traffic or app downloads that cannot be attributed to advertising or other linear marketing efforts; this likely indicates word-of-mouth referrals are operating (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for explaining the lack of trackable invitation mechanism. 1 mark for a valid detection method (exponential homepage traffic without corresponding ad spend is the canonical example).
questions.exam_technique_notes: Two-part question — both parts must be answered.

questions.source_label: Past Paper Example (worked in revision lecture)
questions.question_text: Explain why a company might operate a content-based indirect CGM using company-generated content at a higher frequency than the product's transaction frequency. Why might the company later decide to attempt to transition the CGM to user-generated content?
questions.model_answer: Operating a content CGM at higher than transaction frequency acts as an awareness/retention mechanism — you cannot make users buy more often, but you can keep reminding them the product exists between buying events (1 mark). Company-generated (CG) content is used initially because the company can decide to produce it, often when the user base is too small to generate enough user content, or when content quality must be controlled (1 mark). Transition to user-generated (UG) content later because UG content is more scalable — you only have so many staff or LLM resources, but a large user base can produce content at scale (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for awareness/reminder rationale; 1 mark for why CG (control / early-stage / cannot get users to write yet); 1 mark for scalability rationale of UG.
questions.exam_technique_notes: Two-part question. Common student error: answering only one part.

questions.source_label: Past Paper Example (worked in revision lecture)
questions.question_text: A large, successful consumer internet business with millions of existing users across the world decides to launch a new social media product. To achieve rapid growth, the company implements multiple launch points for the new product within its existing products to convert existing users to also become users of the new product. Within 6 months of launch, the company has acquired tens of millions of users. However, one year later, the active user count is a fraction of this number, and the company closes the product down. With reference to any applicable network effect principles and techniques, give a reasonable explanation as to why this approach was not successful, and suggest a better approach.
questions.model_answer: This is an atomic vs sparse networks problem (1 mark). Although the company moved a large absolute number of users into the new product, those users did not have meaningful relationships with each other ON the new product — it was a sparse network. Without dense, mutually connected users, the network value per user was low, and users churned (real-world examples: Google+ pulling Gmail users, Threads pulling Instagram users). A better approach: build atomic networks first — start with small, dense subgroups (e.g. one university, one workplace, one interest community) where users already have strong mutual connections, prove the network creates value, then expand outward (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for naming/explaining sparse network problem. 1 mark for suggesting atomic network approach (subgroup-by-subgroup growth).
questions.exam_technique_notes: Question signals 'network effect principles' explicitly — that's your starting point.

questions.source_label: Past Paper Example (worked in revision lecture)
questions.question_text: A startup initially operates with one product engineering team that works across all three main areas of its website. During this phase, the product has a consistent design and look-and-feel, but users complain that the features feel unfinished and underpowered. The startup responds by hiring more engineers, so it can split the work into three teams, each dedicated to one of three areas of the product. During this phase, users report the product's depth is stronger, but the product no longer works in a consistent manner across all three areas. Explain which organisational principle or law is applicable here.
questions.model_answer: Conway's Law — organisations ship their organisational structure into the products they build. When the team was unified, the product was consistent but lacked depth. When split into three siloed teams, the team boundaries became product seams, producing inconsistency across areas.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for identifying Conway's Law with brief justification (any words conveying that the product mirrors the org structure).
questions.exam_technique_notes: Only 1 mark — keep answer concise. One sentence sufficient.

questions.source_label: Past Paper Example (worked in revision lecture)
questions.question_text: An early-stage startup has a 6-month LTV of $24. Average cost per acquisition (CPA) is $36. Total additional costs to convert these users into revenue-generating users is $1,200 per month. The startup acquires 100 customers per month. Comment on the company's channel acquisition strategy.
questions.model_answer: Step 1 — Compute additional cost per customer: $1,200 / 100 = $12 (1 mark). Step 2 — Compute total CAC: $36 + $12 = $48 (1 mark). Step 3 — Compute LTV:CAC ratio: $24 / $48 = 0.5, i.e. 1:2 (1 mark). Comment: This ratio is well below the 3:1 healthy threshold, and CAC > LTV — the business loses money on every customer acquired. This is unsustainable as a long-term strategy. However, since this is an early-stage startup, it may be deliberate to (a) generate enough users for statistically valid experiments, (b) spike a CGM in its inertial phase, or (c) build atomic/critical-mass networks. Such an approach is acceptable only as a time-limited strategic investment with a clear endpoint (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Marks for working: extracting per-customer additional cost, computing CAC, computing LTV:CAC. Final mark for nuanced commentary acknowledging both unsustainability AND strategic exception. Showing all working secures partial credit even if final number is wrong.
questions.exam_technique_notes: ALWAYS show working. Even if you make an arithmetic error, method marks are awarded. State the conclusion explicitly.

questions.source_label: Past Paper Example (worked in revision lecture)
questions.question_text: A cohort retention chart for a typical cohort of a SOCIAL MEDIA PRODUCT shows a steep drop during the first 4 weeks (from 100% down to about 20%), then continues to decline gradually to about 12% by week 24. Comment on the cohort retention performance of this product.
questions.model_answer: Description: The initial steep drop is the activation phase — users who do not form a habit are lost (1 mark). After activation, retention declines slowly rather than levelling off, suggesting a 'yellow line' pattern with retention work needed but not catastrophic (1 mark). For a social media product specifically, the activated retention floor should typically be around 60% — this product's activated floor is only ~20%, which is very poor for the category. Activation is the primary problem and should be the focus first; the retention decline is a secondary concern (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for describing what's seen (activation drop + ongoing decline). 1 mark for classifying severity. 1 mark for context-aware comment using the social-media-specific benchmark of ~60% retention after activation.
questions.exam_technique_notes: Pay attention to product type stated in the question — 'social media product' is a clue. Even if uncertain about the benchmark, take a punt: 'I think this is poor for social media' (50/50 to gain a mark, no mark deduction for being wrong).

questions.source_label: Past Paper Example (worked in revision lecture)
questions.question_text: How will ChatGPT and similar products affect the dynamics and economics of content-driven indirect compounding growth mechanisms? Explain your answer.
questions.model_answer: (1) AI lowers the cost of producing content at scale. Company-generated (CG) content CGMs become more like user-generated (UG) ones in terms of scalability — companies can generate content in greater volume more quickly using AI (1 mark). (2) Risk: AI-generated content can be lower quality / repetitive / 'AI slop', and users may object to reading it, so quality control is needed (1 mark). (3) The internet is shifting from search engines to answer engines — users get summaries from LLMs rather than clicking through to source content. Pages-scraped-per-visitor ratios have moved dramatically (Google ~2:1 → 18:1; ChatGPT ~250:1 → 1500:1). This reduces traffic to content, weakening content-based CGM economics (1 mark). (4) Implication: SEO-dependent content CGMs face declining performance; more businesses buy ads to compensate, raising ad costs and making money-based CGMs harder to operate profitably. Content CGMs may retain value as in-platform retention mechanisms (e.g. Medium, LinkedIn) rather than acquisition mechanisms (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Approximately 1 mark per substantive AI-impact point. Strong answers cover both supply-side (easier to generate) and demand-side (search-to-answer shift) impacts.
questions.exam_technique_notes: Note the word 'Explain' — give reasons, not just descriptions. ChatGPT is a confirmed exam product.

questions.source_label: Past Paper Example (worked in revision lecture)
questions.question_text: List each of the network effects and compounding growth mechanisms present in the growth model for TikTok. For each item, state its type and provide a brief description of its operation.
questions.model_answer: Network Effects: (1) 2-sided network: content creators ↔ viewers — creators attracted by audience, viewers attracted by content. (2) 2-sided network: advertisers ↔ viewers — advertisers attracted by audience size and targeting; viewers tolerate ads as price of free content. [Note: can alternatively be described as one 3-sided network across creators+viewers+advertisers.] (3) Data network effect: more usage data → better recommendation algorithm → more relevant feed → more retention and use. (4) Scale-based effects: brand recognition / purchasing power for infrastructure deals. CGMs: (5) Content-based indirect CGM (UG): users create short videos; videos are shared to other platforms (Instagram, Twitter, WhatsApp) and bring new users to TikTok. (6) Organic direct CGM: word-of-mouth recommendations ('check out this TikTok'). (7) Possibly a direct CGM via in-app share/invite feature if implemented. Approximately 1 mark per correctly named-and-described mechanism, up to a max of 6 marks.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per correctly named AND briefly described mechanism. Naming alone (e.g. 'network effect') without specifying type or describing operation will not score full marks. Listing 6 mechanisms is the target; listing 7-8 provides safety margin against errors.
questions.exam_technique_notes: 6 marks → aim for 6 distinct mechanisms (or 7-8 to be safe). Name properly (e.g. '2-sided network' not just 'network effect') and describe the operation in context of the product.

questions.question_text: Describe the three main types of Acquisition channels.
questions.model_answer: (1) Intent-based channels: users are searching with intent to buy or otherwise complete an action (e.g. SEO, SEM). (2) Awareness-based channels: users do not have intent at the point where ads are presented (e.g. Facebook ads, TV). (3) Referral-based mechanisms: bring new users who have accepted invitations from other users or been indirectly referred to the product (CGMs).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per channel type correctly named and described.

questions.question_text: Contrast the conversion performance of the three main types of acquisition.
questions.model_answer: Awareness-based channels have the lowest conversion performance (1 mark). Intent and Referral-based mechanisms usually have relatively high conversion performance (1 mark). Referral-based conversion depends on factors such as referrer credibility and the configuration of the referral mechanism (e.g. perceived value of any financial incentive) (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per substantive contrast point.

questions.question_text:
A start-up records the following acquisition performance during a typical month:
(1) Cost of Google SEM Marketing: $154,000
(2) Cost of Facebook Ads: $32,000
(3) Cost of Affiliate Marketing channel: $85,000
(4) Google SEM additional total costs in converting customers to revenue after acquisition: $8,000
(5) Facebook Ads additional total costs: $14,000
(6) Affiliate Marketing additional total costs: $12,000
(7) Google SEM customers acquired: 1,155
(8) Facebook Ads customers acquired: 45
(9) Affiliate Marketing customers acquired: 480
(10) Google SEM typical retention period: 15 months
(11) Facebook Ads typical retention period: 11 months
(12) Affiliate Marketing typical retention period: 13 months
(13) Typical monthly revenue: $42
State which of these channels has the best performance, justifying your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculate LTV:CAC for each channel.
Google SEM: CAC = ($154,000 + $8,000) / 1,155 = $140.25; LTV = $42 × 15 = $630; LTV:CAC = 630/140.25 = 4.5 (2 marks)
Facebook Ads: CAC = ($32,000 + $14,000) / 45 = $1,022.22; LTV = $42 × 11 = $462; LTV:CAC = 462/1,022.22 = 0.45 (1 mark)
Affiliate: CAC = ($85,000 + $12,000) / 480 = $202.08; LTV = $42 × 13 = $546; LTV:CAC = 546/202.08 = 2.7 (1 mark)
Google SEM has the best performance due to highest LTV:CAC ratio (4.5) (1 mark). (No marks for stating answer without calculation.)
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Marks for working out each channel's LTV:CAC + final ranking. Show working — no marks for naked answer.

questions.question_text: You join a start-up as the Growth Director. On your first day, the team boasts to you about an LTV:CAC ratio of 6:1. What questions would you ask, in order to determine the accuracy of this claim?
questions.model_answer: (1) What costs are included between the point of acquisition and the point of revenue generation? (1 mark). (2) Is the CAC segmented by channel and, if so, are we referring to a specific channel or blended-channel CAC? (1 mark). (3) Is the CAC segmented by customer type and, if so, are we referring to a specific customer type or blended-customer CAC? (1 mark). (4) What lifetime value is being used in the calculation, and what assumptions are being made regarding the average revenue per customer and retention period? What data supports those assumptions? (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per substantive diligence question (any 4 of the canonical issues: cost coverage, channel segmentation, customer segmentation, LTV assumptions/retention period).

questions.question_text: Explain why businesses aim to achieve an LTV:CAC ratio of at least 3:1.
questions.model_answer: If CAC > LTV, the acquisition activity loses money on each customer, which is unsustainable (1 mark). LTV being equal to or slightly greater than CAC is insufficient because the business has many other overheads and fixed costs not included in CAC; a ratio of 3:1 or above generally enables profitability after accounting for these costs (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the unsustainability of CAC > LTV; 1 mark for the headroom-for-fixed-costs argument.

questions.question_text: Explain how Growth teams use the Activation Inequality to optimise product activation performance.
questions.model_answer: The Activation Inequality asserts that the value perceived by the user must be greater than the effort perceived to realise that value, otherwise the user will be lost before Stage 1 of Activation is completed (1 mark). Growth and design teams use it when considering, for example, the ordering of steps in the activation process and the amount of information requested from users before delivering value to them (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for stating the inequality; 1 mark for at least one concrete application (step ordering / info-gathering reduction).

questions.question_text: A start-up's activation workflow includes a step that requires the new user to grant access to the user's phone contact list. It then encourages the user to invite friends to use the app before the user can start using the app fully. Comment on the pros and cons of this approach.
questions.model_answer: Pros: likely drives a higher level of referral; users start the referral process before establishing a habit, so even those who do not activate still contribute to referrals. Cons: increases the friction of activation (violates Activation Inequality by adding effort before value), so likely reduces activation rate; delays providing value to the user, also damaging activation. (1 mark for any of these, up to a maximum of 2 marks.)
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Up to 2 marks for substantive pros AND cons. A balanced answer covering both sides scores higher.

questions.question_text: A cohort retention chart shows seven sequential cohorts of a product, where Cohort 1 is the earliest and Cohort 7 is the latest. The activation performance of the cohorts has been steadily improving from Cohort 1 to Cohort 5. However, in Cohorts 6 and 7, ongoing retention performance shows a new decline. Comment on the cohort trend shown, giving examples of what could be driving this trend.
questions.model_answer: Activation performance for the product is improving over time across the cohort sequence (1 mark). A likely explanation is that the start-up is experimenting with activation workflow improvements (1 mark). In Cohorts 6 and 7, there is a new decline in ongoing retention performance (1 mark). This could have been caused by an experiment or feature introduction that has damaged retention — e.g. a recently shipped change to the core experience or a degraded onboarding step (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Marks for: identifying improving activation, plausible explanation, identifying late-cohort retention regression, plausible cause for regression.

questions.question_text: Explain the composition (i.e. the structure) of a retention metric. How do Growth teams decide which specific retention metric to use?
questions.model_answer: Structure: NaP, where N = number of times an action is performed, a = the name of the action, P = the period in which it is performed. The metric quantifies the intensity and frequency of an action that correlates most strongly with future user retention (2 marks for the structural points). Setting the metric: examine how actions at given frequencies and intensities correlate with future retention; the stronger the correlation, the better the candidate metric (1 mark). In early stages where there is insufficient traffic or time, choose a reasonable candidate and refine over time (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 2 marks for structure (NaP definition); 1 mark for correlation-based selection; 1 mark for early-stage refinement strategy.

questions.question_text: A Retention-Cohort Table for a product shows the number of customers still active in each of the weeks following sign-up, across multiple cohorts. By examining the data, comment on the cohort trend and provide a reasonable interpretation. What action should the team take? (Note: this question type is unlikely in the current exam since data download is no longer permitted, but the question is still useful for revision.)
questions.model_answer: Transpose the absolute counts into a cohort percentage decay table (normalised to either previous month or base month) — this exposes patterns hidden in absolute numbers (1 mark). The decay table will show whether activation has worsened (e.g. one cohort with notably worse early retention) or whether ongoing retention has changed. If Cohort 7 (or the most recent) shows worse activation, this is most likely due to a recent change in the product's activation flow or marketing activities (1 mark). The team should: review all experiments, feature changes, and marketing activity changes introduced at that time, and determine whether a change needs rolling back; also check seasonal and external market factors (2 marks).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for normalisation strategy; 1 mark for diagnosing activation regression; 2 marks for action plan (experiment review + rollback + external factor check).
questions.exam_technique_notes: Per Mark Logan: this question form is no longer used in exams since data downloads are not permitted. Useful for revision only.

questions.question_text: Comment on the suitability of the following retention metric for a Tax Return Calculation package: 4r28, where r = review tax details.
questions.model_answer: This is an inappropriate metric for most months of the year because tax products tend to be used yearly — both the period (28 days) and the number of uses (4) are too frequent in general (1 mark). However, during the tax-return season itself, this metric may be more appropriate as users genuinely review their details multiple times across a few weeks (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for identifying the mismatch with annual usage; 1 mark for the seasonal nuance.

questions.question_text: Explain why Growth teams sometimes use two different content-based Indirect CGM subtypes in sequence, as part of a growth strategy.
questions.model_answer: There are two main sub-types of Content-based indirect CGM: Company-Generated content (CG) and User-Generated content (UG) (1 mark). CG is easier to move through the inertial phase but harder to scale; UG has the opposite characteristics. Combining them in sequence — start with CG, then add UG — captures the advantages of both (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for identifying both sub-types; 1 mark for the start-CG-then-UG rationale.

questions.question_text: Explain how a start-up should decide which sub-type of Direct Compounding Growth Mechanism is likely to be most effective for its product.
questions.model_answer: Three sub-types exist: Personal Utility-based, Financial, and Social Capital-based (1 mark). A start-up where users experience significant benefit from the referral itself (in terms of subsequent product value, e.g. messaging apps) prefers a Personal Utility model (1 mark). The Financial sub-type is better when no such 'selfish benefit' exists. Social Capital effects often supplement the first two but can drive referral when no direct benefit exists and the business model cannot sustain a financial mechanism (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Up to 3 marks for explaining the three sub-types and the criteria for choosing among them.

questions.question_text: Explain the relationship between Business-Model <-> Channel Fit and Financial Asymmetry in financially-incentivised Compounding Growth Mechanisms.
questions.model_answer: Business-Model <-> Channel Fit requires that the cost of acquiring customers through a channel is sustainably supportable by the revenue earned from those customers. If a CGM's financial incentive is too large relative to LTV, this requirement is not met and the mechanism will ultimately lose the business money. Financial Asymmetry — where the perceived value of the incentive to the user can exceed the actual cost to the business (e.g. a free month of a subscription product) — helps make financial CGMs viable while preserving Business-Model <-> Channel Fit.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Marks for explaining the constraint (BM-channel fit) AND the lever (asymmetry) that allows financial incentives to remain affordable.

questions.question_text: Explain what is meant by the Starvation Phase of a Compounding Growth Loop. What action should the start-up take during this phase: continue as before, increase time optimising this mechanism, or reduce focus on the mechanism? Why?
questions.model_answer: In the starvation phase, the number of potential new users reachable by the mechanism begins to saturate (1 mark). Maintaining the same strategy as in the growth phase yields diminishing results, as would increasing focus (1 mark). Better to redirect resources to either establishing a new mechanism, changing the market in which the mechanism operates, or another significant contextual change — i.e. reduce focus on this mechanism (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the saturation explanation; 1 mark for the diminishing-returns logic; 1 mark for the redirect action and rationale.

questions.question_text: Explain the operation of an n-sided network. Give an example of a well-known product based on an n-sided network as part of your answer.
questions.model_answer: In general network effects, the greater the participation in the network, the greater the value to its participants — which attracts further participants in a self-reinforcing loop (1 mark). In an n-sided network, there are n types of participant; one type acts as an attractor for other types (1 mark). Example: Facebook consists of users, advertisers, and content providers. The presence of users attracts content providers; content from those providers attracts additional users; both attract advertisers (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the basic network-effects concept; 1 mark for the n-sided structure; 1 mark for a valid example with explanation.

questions.question_text: Explain how start-ups attempt to manage liquidity in the earliest stages of a 2-sided network's lifetime.
questions.model_answer: Liquidity in a 2-sided network concerns ensuring sufficient and balanced supply and demand. In an early-stage network, there is usually a lack of both (1 mark for explaining the basic problem). Supply-side techniques: incentivise suppliers to join, compensate them for lack of earnings, actively recruit (1 mark for two examples). Demand-side techniques: drive referral mechanisms with incentives, unsustainable advertising, discounting (1 mark for two examples).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the liquidity problem; 1 mark for two supply-side techniques; 1 mark for two demand-side techniques.

questions.question_text: Explain how, in a 2-sided network, network effects can strengthen the growth performance of compounding growth mechanisms at the demand-side of the network.
questions.model_answer: The 2-sided network attracts more users to the demand-side because they are drawn by the available supply on the other side (1 mark). This means the demand-side CGM is acting upon a greater number of users in each iteration, generating more returns per cycle (1 mark). Network attraction also creates more impetus for referred users to join the product, since the perceived value of joining is higher when supply is plentiful (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Marks for: (1) network attraction increases demand-side population; (2) more users in each CGM iteration → more output; (3) higher join intent for referees due to value of network.

questions.question_text: Explain why compounding growth mechanisms rarely work well on the supply-side of a 2-sided network, in contrast to the demand-side, where they are often very effective.
questions.model_answer: At the supply-side, participants are often in competition with each other; there is little or no incentive operating that would drive referral behaviour.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the competition-disincentive explanation.

questions.question_text: Explain, with reference to any applicable principles, why it is very difficult for an organization that is highly focussed on its internal functional hierarchy to successfully optimize the Growth Model's Customer Journey.
questions.model_answer: The Customer Journey requires multiple skillsets to work closely together AND requires the organisation to focus on this process continuously. This is harder if the organisation is structured around skill-based silos and does not routinely combine people from different skill-areas into teams (2 marks). Conway's Law: organisations tend to mirror their organisational structures in the products they build (1 mark). In this case, Conway's Law predicts that a purely functional hierarchy will create interfaces between teams that disrupt the requirement to work as a single integrated team on the Customer Journey (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 2 marks for the multi-skill / sustained-focus argument; 1 mark for stating Conway's Law; 1 mark for applying it to this scenario.

questions.question_text: In the context of the Lean Start-up methodology, what properties distinguish Learning Metrics from Vanity Metrics?
questions.model_answer: Learning Metrics: express a measure of activity; therefore frequency-based. Vanity Metrics: typically simple accumulators with no relationship to frequency.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Marks for the activity/frequency vs accumulator distinction.

questions.question_text: A founding team of a small start-up iterates rapidly by quickly making all of the decisions in the business. This is very effective. However, when the team grows to 40 people in size, the CEO realises that, despite working the same way as before, the speed of iteration of the business has considerably reduced. Explain what is most probably causing this velocity reduction.
questions.model_answer: The business is slowing because decisions are being overly centralised at a scale where this model no longer fits (1 mark). Decision latency has increased, and decision intensity drops proportional to the SQUARE of decision latency, significantly reducing iteration speed (1 mark). This also affects employee morale and sense of agency, further reducing iteration speed; eventually the founders become overloaded, worsening the problem (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for centralisation; 1 mark for decision latency / decision intensity; 1 mark for compounding effects (morale, overload).

questions.question_text: With reference to the previous question, what general approach should the founders consider to improve the performance of the business on a sustainable basis going forward?
questions.model_answer: Push agency to the front-line of the business, as an organisational strategic goal. (Half mark for 'they should make less decisions themselves' or similar without naming the agency principle.)
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for naming agency-pushing as the strategic answer; half-mark for the weaker formulation.

questions.question_text: Explain the differences between the investment stages Seed, Series A and Series B.
questions.model_answer: These stages relate to different growth points in a start-up. Seed capital is typically less than $2 million, corresponding to the stage where the start-up is seeking product-market fit. Series A is typically awarded to drive growth and is of the order of $10 million. Series B ($30m+) and later stages are typically larger, to further drive growth.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Marks for distinguishing each stage by typical size and company stage.

questions.question_text: The concept of growth models doesn't just apply to modern tech start-ups and scale-ups. Disney Corporation has been described historically using a growth-flywheel diagram (Walt Disney, 1957). More recently, Disney launched the Disney+ streaming service. Using your knowledge of this service and any available material you can find on the internet, describe the growth model for Disney+.
questions.model_answer: Up to 5 marks for any 5 of: (1) Aggregator Effect: Disney+ is the only streaming service where all Disney assets can be viewed, attracting Disney fans; the more content Disney creates, the stronger this effect. (2) Money-based CGM: subscription revenue → buy ads → sign-ups → subscription revenue, often spiked with extra paid-marketing spend to seed other CGMs. (3) Organic direct CGM: subscription revenue → fund new content → users watch and tell friends by word-of-mouth → some sign up. (4) Content-based indirect CGM: account sharing with up to 7 users (4 simultaneous devices) eventually creates pressure for some users to sign up for their own account. (5) Activation/Activation Inequality: free trial period demonstrates value before requiring payment. (6) Engagement Intensity: regular new content (movies, box sets), Group Watch feature, in-app recommendation engine, auto-start next episode, regular emails, multiple user profiles.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for each of any 5 distinct mechanisms (or similar). Listing 6+ provides safety margin.
questions.exam_technique_notes: 5 marks → aim for 5+ mechanisms. Always name the mechanism type AND describe its operation in the product's context.

questions.question_text: Swipii is an app-based start-up that enables shoppers to receive cash-back when they make purchases in shops. New users first link their debit cards then sign up. Whenever they shop in a Swipii-affiliated store, they receive cashback into their Swipii account. Businesses can offer special offers (e.g. 10% cashback on a coffee purchased before 10:00am on a Tuesday). Swipii is therefore a two-sided network of shoppers and shops. When Swipii enters a new country, which is the better strategy: target some shops across as many cities as possible, or focus on just one or two cities at a time? Explain your answer.
questions.model_answer: Swipii should concentrate on one or two cities at a time. (1) Referral mechanisms work better with critical mass, which is more achievable when efforts are concentrated in one city (1 mark). (2) As a 2-sided network, it is easier to create an Atomic Network in a small area first; once it is proven, expansion is easier (1 mark). Credit also given for: focusing on one city makes it easier to learn and test user experience quickly to establish PMF in the new market.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the referral/critical-mass argument; 1 mark for the atomic-network argument. Alternative: PMF/learning-speed argument also creditable.

questions.question_text: An early-stage start-up acquires 1,500 customers a month on average, at an average CPA of $80. The start-up uses a sales team to convert customer leads to revenue-generating customers, at a total salary cost of $120,000 per year. The start-up estimates its 6-month customer LTV to be $300. Comment on the company's channel acquisition strategy.
questions.model_answer: 6-month LTV = $300. Channel acquisition cost per customer = $80. Additional sales cost per customer = $120,000 / (12 × 1,500) = $6.67 per customer (1 mark). Total CAC = $80 + $6.67 = $86.67 (1 mark). LTV:CAC = 300 / 86.67 = 3.46 (1 mark). The ratio exceeds 3:1, meaning acquisition is profitable with headroom to cover other fixed costs. The acquisition strategy is sound (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 3 marks for the calculation chain; 1 mark for the soundness conclusion with reference to the 3:1 threshold.

questions.question_text: Explain why Intent-based channels usually exhibit a higher conversion rate than Awareness-based channels. Why are Awareness-based channels still used despite this difference in conversion rates?
questions.model_answer: Intent-based channels reach users who are already searching with intent to buy or complete an action; awareness-based channels reach users without current intent (1 mark). Awareness-based channels are still used because they build brand awareness and reduce the likelihood that users forget about the business — they also typically improve performance of intent-based channels by making the brand recognisable when users do search (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for each part.

questions.question_text: In what circumstances is it appropriate to operate with CAC > LTV?
questions.model_answer: It is appropriate to do this for limited periods in order to generate users for the purposes of conducting statistically valid experiments or to 'spike' a CGM in its inertial phase.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the time-limited strategic-investment rationale (experiments OR CGM spiking are both valid).

questions.question_text: Explain what is meant by the Inertial Phase of a Compounding Growth mechanism. Provide one example from each of two separate businesses (i.e. two examples in total) of approaches to overcome this inertia.
questions.model_answer: At the start of a CGM's lifecycle, it is often more difficult to encourage users to refer other users and for users to act on invitations to sign-up — referrers are reluctant to recommend an unknown brand, invitees are reluctant to join a product with few members (1 mark). Example 1 — Uber: temporarily operated unsustainably (subsidising drivers, advertising spend) in new cities to build critical mass of supply and demand (1 mark). Example 2 — Electric scooter start-ups (e.g. Lime): geo-concentrated their entire fleet in one small area of a city, creating visible density and critical mass before expanding (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the inertial-phase explanation; 1 mark per valid concrete example using temporary unprofitability OR geo-concentration tactics.

questions.question_text: A cohort retention chart shows the performance of seven sequential newly acquired user cohorts. Cohorts 1-3 improve steadily. Cohort 4 performs relatively badly during activation and then recovers somewhat. Cohorts 5-7 resume the improvement trend, with some Cohort 4 users moving out of dormancy in later periods. Comment on the sequence and provide an explanation for any anomalies.
questions.model_answer: Generally the cohorts are improving over time, perhaps due to ongoing product improvement (1 mark). However, Cohort 4 is out of sequence — performing poorly during activation and partially recovering thereafter (1 mark). Possible explanation: a bug or other issue temporarily introduced into the activation flow during that period, or an external event (e.g. holiday, market event, outage) that distracted users or reduced product use; this is supported by the fact that later cohorts return to the improvement trend AND some Cohort 4 users move out of dormancy later (2 marks).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for general improvement; 1 mark for identifying the Cohort 4 anomaly; 2 marks for a plausible mechanism that explains BOTH the activation dip AND the eventual recovery / later cohort restoration.

questions.question_text: A growth team constructs a Quantitative Growth Model for its product, an n-sided network based trading platform. Explain what future trend you would incorporate into the quantitative model for linear acquisition for this product.
questions.model_answer: This is a moving variable question. (1) As network effects strengthen, linear acquisition performance starts to improve due to those network effects — it becomes easier to attract new users (1 mark). (2) Eventually, as the market begins to saturate, acquisition performance stabilises and then drops over time (1 mark). I.e. an 'improve then diminish' pattern.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per phase of the moving variable (improvement then decline).

questions.question_text: Explain the relationship between network effects and compounding growth mechanisms.
questions.model_answer: Network effects and CGMs are not the same mechanism. (1) Network effects attract participants — but the attractor is not a referral mechanism (1 mark). (2) CGMs are referral-based mechanisms; they can be accelerated by network effects, can accelerate network effects, but can operate independently of network effects (1 mark for all of point 2).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for stating they are not the same; 1 mark for the mutual-amplification-yet-independence point.

questions.question_text: A founder-CEO of a rapidly growing technology start-up laments to her co-founders that engineers don't release features as quickly as was the case when she and her co-founders were doing all the work, and that everything just seems to take longer now. She concludes that the problem is that the quality of people the company is hiring must be the issue. Comment on her conclusion and suggest what action she should take first.
questions.model_answer: The CEO may be correct, but it is more likely that there is a system-level problem caused by organisational growth. The CEO should first assess agency among front-line staff (1 mark for considering agency). Specifically check: (1) Is everyone clear about what their job is and what decisions they own? (2) Are people competent in their current roles, recognising that competence degrades with scale unless invested in? (3) Are people well-aligned to the strategy and goals of the business? (4) Do they have access to the skills and resources they need? (1 mark for exploring components of agency). She should next check the performance of key processes in the business, and whether they have degraded. Only if all of the above checks out well should she consider individual staff capability — some staff may have 'scaled out' and cannot operate well in a larger business (1 mark for general quality and depth).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for considering agency; 1 mark for exploring components of agency (any of competence/ownership/alignment/resources); 1 mark for general quality and depth, including the systems-before-individuals reasoning.

questions.question_text: What are the three typical patterns shown on a retention-cohort graph? For each, state what it indicates about the business.
questions.model_answer: (1) Green line — drops then levels off; users have formed habits and retention has stabilised; if most cohorts look like this, the business has PMF. (2) Yellow line — continues falling slowly; retention is not catastrophic but needs improvement; common in early-stage start-ups. (3) Red line — falls rapidly toward zero; the business is heading for failure unless retention is significantly improved.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per pattern correctly described and interpreted.

questions.question_text: Explain the structure of a retention metric (NaP). Give two rules for setting a good NaP metric and explain why each rule matters.
questions.model_answer: Structure: NaP — N = number of times an action is performed, a = the specific action, P = the time period in days (1 mark for structure). Rule 1: N should be greater than 1, because this gives a better signal-to-noise ratio and reduces false churn signals — if N=1, a single missed action would falsely flag a user as churning (1.5 marks). Rule 2: P should be greater than the typical usage cycle of the product. For example, if the product is used mainly on weekdays, P=1 day would create false churn signals on weekends (1.5 marks).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for structure; up to 1.5 marks per rule with explanation of why it matters.

questions.question_text: A tax return software company uses the retention metric 4r28 (4 tax reviews every 28 days). Comment on the suitability of this metric.
questions.model_answer: Inappropriate for most months because tax products are typically used yearly; both N=4 and P=28 days are far too frequent for natural usage frequency (1 mark). However, during tax-return season, the metric may be more appropriate as users may legitimately review tax details multiple times across a few weeks (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for natural-frequency mismatch; 1 mark for seasonal appropriateness.

questions.question_text: Explain the Activation Inequality. How do growth teams use it to optimise onboarding?
questions.model_answer: Perceived Value > Perceived Effort. If the effort required to start using the product exceeds the value the user perceives, they will be lost before activating (1 mark). Growth teams use it to optimise the ordering of steps in activation and to minimise the amount of information requested before delivering value — value demonstration should come before heavy info gathering (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the inequality; 1 mark for at least one application.

questions.question_text: A startup's activation workflow requires users to grant access to their phone contact list and invite friends BEFORE they can fully use the app. Discuss the pros and cons.
questions.model_answer: Pros: drives higher referral levels because every user goes through the referral step; even users who don't fully activate contribute referrals. Cons: increases friction (violates Activation Inequality by adding effort before value), reducing activation rate; delays providing value to the user, also damaging activation.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Up to 2 marks for substantive pros AND cons.

questions.question_text: A delivery app uses 4o28 as its retention metric. Describe how you would categorise users into Power, Core, and Churn-risk categories. What action should the team take when a user moves from Core to Churn-risk?
questions.model_answer: Power user: (6+)o28 — 6 or more orders every 28 days; deepest habit, most valuable. Core user: (4-5)o28 — meeting or slightly exceeding the retention threshold; healthy. Churn-risk: (<4)o28 — below threshold (1.5 marks for categorisation). When a user drops from Core to Churn-risk, trigger immediate intervention: targeted offers, push notifications, personalised recommendations, or discounts to re-engage them before they fully churn (1.5 marks for action).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1.5 marks for category boundaries; 1.5 marks for substantive intervention plan.

questions.question_text: Explain the difference between Direct and Indirect CGMs. Give one example of each type from a real product.
questions.model_answer: Direct CGMs: users directly invite other users — currency = users themselves. Example: WhatsApp — users invite friends so they can message them (personal-utility direct CGM) (1.5 marks). Indirect CGMs: an intermediate currency (content or money) attracts new users; the user may not even be aware they are attracting new users. Example: Medium — users write articles that are shared via social media and discovered via SEO, attracting new readers (content-based indirect CGM) (1.5 marks).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1.5 marks per type with definition and product example.

questions.question_text: A CGM has V = 0.52. Calculate the Growth Multiplier. If an experiment improves V to 0.58, what is the new Growth Multiplier? Comment on the significance of this improvement.
questions.model_answer: GM = 1/(1-V). With V=0.52: GM = 1/(1-0.52) = 1/0.48 = 2.08 (1 mark). With V=0.58: GM = 1/(1-0.58) = 1/0.42 = 2.38 (1 mark). The improvement from 2.08 to 2.38 (~14% uplift in GM) results from only a 6 percentage-point increase in V — demonstrating compounding: small improvements in CGM conversion parameters amplify through the loop into disproportionately large gains (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per GM calc; 1 mark for the compounding-significance commentary.

questions.question_text: Explain why a product with very strong organic word-of-mouth CGMs might not need classical linear marketing, while most startups do.
questions.model_answer: Linear marketing provides initial users to 'seed' CGMs — without it, CGMs have no users to operate upon. The analogy: linear marketing is the 'flame' that ignites compounding growth, or the 'principal' upon which compounding 'interest' is earned. Products with very strong organic word-of-mouth (e.g. early WhatsApp) generate enough organic referrals that no additional seeding is needed (1 mark). Most startups have CGMs that require initial user volume to achieve momentum, and organic word-of-mouth alone is insufficient. Hence most startups need linear marketing to reach the critical mass where CGMs begin to compound (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the seeding/flame/principal concept; 1 mark for why most startups still need linear marketing.
